title: Bush Tucker Dreaming
material: synthetic polymer paint on composition board
description: Bush Tucker Dreaming synthetic polymer paint on composition board 18 x 11 7/8 in (45.7 x 30.1 cm) Painted in 1971
provenance: Stuart Art Centre, Alice Springs no. 14031. | Corbally Stourton Contemporary Art, London. | Private collection, UK. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Literature | P.C. Stourton, Songlines and Dreamings: Contemporary Australian Aboriginal Painting, London, 1996, no. 1 (illustrated p. 30). | G. Bardon, J. Bardon, Papunya, A Place Made After the Story: The Beginnings of the Western Desert Painting Movement, Victoria, Australia, 2004, no. 255 (illustrated p. 315) (titled Yam Dreaming). | | | | Bardon's publication, which includes this work, documents the genesis of the Western Desert painting movement from 1971 until 1973. Bardon's support and enthusiasm fueled the works of a handful of founding artists; that momentum resulting in the formation of the Papunya Tula Artists company. Most of the artists from that powerful 'painting mob' have passed away, though their children and grandchildren are now amongst Australia's leading artists with exhibitions scheduled around the globe. | | Bardon methodically preserved field notes and schematic drawings of works at the time of the execution. Pushing against the then heavy tide of institutionalized racism, Bardon recognized that something momentous was occurring and quietly worked to document it. | | Anatjari Tjakamarra, also known as Anatjari No. III, was a Pintupi man of considerable grace. He was amongst the first of the Western Desert men to commence painting at Papunya in 1971. An artist of particular ability, Anatjari has his own workspace under curved corrugated iron roof of the Nissen Hut that was the 'Men's Painting Room', a space that 'buzzed with excitement as men of high standing came together to paint a constellation of sites distributed across a broad band of country.' (1) | | This work, known as 'Yam Dreaming' and 'Bush Tucker Dreaming', is accompanied by the following field notes from the time of its painting on page 315 of Bardon, | | 'The concentric circles with loops represent yam plants with yams in the ground; other concentric circles represent fires, and the Yam Dreaming is indicated by ceremonial objects. This Pintupi artist's figuration for the yam plant differ from the pictographic shapes of his fellow Pintupi, Charlie Tarawa (Tjaruru) Tjungurrayi, yet each conceptualization was consistent with the emphatically ceremonial nature of the story, which included large, undisguised and culturally explicit ceremonial objects. Anatjari has made the ceremony and ideograms of the plant of a conceptual size appropriate to the story both told and enacted.' | | Bardon dedicated the book, which remains an essential reference for this most important movement, to; | | 'Those twenty-five or more towering artists of my experience of the Western Desert, and to all their marvelous kith and kin; but also, it is a justification, amply and I hope, unforgettably seen, of what in the darkness of time sometimes can be mislaid and lost, because it was not understood for what it was. Give to the innocent that which is their due.' | | | 1. John Kean, 'Framing Papunya Painting: Form, Style and Representation, 1971 – 72' in Luke Scholes, Tjungunutja: From Having Come Together, Museum and Art Gallery of Northern Territory, Darwin, 2017, p. 192

title: An Ounce of Luck
description: An Ounce of Luck signed 'Ernie Barnes' (lower right) acrylic on canvas 20 x 24 in (50.8 x 61 cm) Painted in 1989
provenance: Private collection, New Hampshire (acquired from the artist in 1989). | | Literature | W. Lowe, Jr., 'An Ounce of Luck,' Playboy, September 1989, vol. 36, no. 9 (illustrated p. 80-81). | | | Ernie Barnes has never strayed far from the American cultural consciousness. Sports professionals, movie stars and musicians alike have commissioned and acquired paintings by the artist; his paintings were, perhaps most famously to the public eye, a title image for the classic sitcom "Good Times" (1974-1979); the cover of Marvin Gaye's 1976 album "I Want You", and The Crusaders 1984 album "Ghetto Blaster." His significance, therefore, as a cultural staple of late 20th century America is a fact only recently coming into clarity. His life and art have been the subject of retrospectives at the California African American Museum in summer 2019, and a recent New York Times piece described his canvases as "domains of earnestness and striving, of unalloyed celebration and pride. This might mistakenly be read as unsophisticated or naïve, when in fact it is principled, even defiant", and Barnes himself "an artist of the people – most especially of Black people" (Adam Bradley, 'Millions Saw His Paintings on TV. In the Art World, His Work Still Went Unnoticed', The New York Times, 15 September 2023, Online). His impact and the beauty of his paintings cannot be divided from his legacy as a champion of the Black experience and the American history of twentieth century painting. | | The present lot was painted to accompany a short story of the same name submitted to Playboy's September 1989 issue. The story, written by Walter Lowe, Jr., revolves around a bet made between Alfred Toomey III and "the Nigerian." The story opens in a casino, where Toomey III has been dominating a game of five-card draw. Toomey III asserts that money can buy anything, including luck. The Nigerian, however, denies this assertion, eventually revealing that he is in possession of three small beads which hang in a small bag around his neck and, according to him, contain luck that is released upon the bead being consumed. Toomey III's skepticism is quickly put to the test when the two agree that the Nigerian will demonstrate the power of the beads through three daring feats, each constructed by Toomey, in exchange for $130,000,000 in gold. | | The Nigerian passes each test thanks to the beads and quickly convinces Toomey III that the magic power stored within them is real. However, the story takes shape as a fable once Toomey acquires his own bag of beads through deceit. The reader is taken through a whiplash sequence of events that culminate in Toomey III in the hospital believing himself broke. The Nigerian visits him and explains that the beads contain luck, but half of them are good luck, and half are bad. He goes on to explain that he had deduced how many of each he had left after testing them out with the same fervor as Toomey III and knew when he met Toomey that night in the casino that his last three were good luck. He reiterates his original assertion that luck cannot be purchased, and even when one tries, there's no guarantee that they are purchasing good luck. | | Ernie Barnes' signature style is not only well illustrated in An Ounce of Luck but is also enriched by the framing structure of Lowe's story. The tall, lean figures of the main characters dominate the foreground, and in his positioning of them, Barnes highlights clearly their differences in disposition. His stylized approach to the human form is on full display in An Ounce of Luck, as is his talent for small details that create a narrative in place of the distinct facial features and architectural settings that the artist often foregoes. The musculature in each of their strained necks, the pointed feet and long spindly arms readily call upon Barnes' classic depictions of athletes. A chorus of Barnes' talent, it is a splendid and prominently published example by one of the great painters of everyday life in the twentieth century.

title: Untitled (Figure With Still Life)
description: Untitled (Figure With Still Life) oil on canvas 40 x 48 1/4 in (101.6 x 122.5 cm) Painted in 1958-1959
provenance: Estate of the artist, New York. | The Judith Rothschild Foundation, New York. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. |  | Born in New York City in 1921, Judith Rothschild was fully immersed in the milieu of Post-War Abstraction that infused the city in the 1940s and 1950s. While studying art at Wellesley College, Cranbook Academy and the Art Students League, she further honed her craft alongside names like Reginald Marsh and Hans Hofmann. In 1945, she became a member of the Jane Street group along with fellow artists Jane Freilicher, Larry Rivers and Nell Blaine, subsequently debuting her first solo exhibition at Jane Street Gallery, the first cooperative New York artists' gallery, in December of that year. |  | Rothschild's unique style, which hints at figures, objects or landscapes, is executed with the bravura of an abstractionist. As demonstrated in her 1950's canvases, her abstraction is grounded in a unique vision that often draws from natural forms. Like many female artists of the period, in a predominantly male art world, Rothschild faced significant challenges in gaining recognition. In addition to her long-standing career as a painter, she became a champion of underrepresented artists in her later life. Today, she is finally gaining the much-deserved market recognition for her own work as an abstract artist.   |  | While Judith Rothschild's market recognition is a more recent phenomenon, her institutional recognition is well-established. Her work is included in the collections of more than 50 institutions worldwide, including Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum; The Metropolitan Museum of Art; National Gallery of Art; Whitney Museum of American Art; Museum of Modern Art; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Philadelphia Museum of Art; The Phillips Collection, Washington, D.C.; Tate Modern, London; Musee National d'art Moderne, Paris; Centre Pompidou, Paris; and Sammlung Ludwig Museum, Aachen, Germany.

provenance: Collection of Ralph Humphrey, New York. | Bykert Gallery, New York. | Peder Bonnier Ltd, New York. | Collection of Andy Warhol, New York. | Sale: Sotheby's, New York, Andy Warhol Collection, 2-3 May 1988, Lot 3369. | Private collection, Antwerp. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | New York, Bykert Gallery, Brice Marden: Back Series, January 6 - 31, 1968. | New York, Vivian Horan Fine Art, Minimalism: On and Off Paper, September 28 - November 17, 2006. | Minneapolis, Minneapolis Institute of Art, December 2006 - circa October 2014 (on extended loan). | | Literature | L. Encrevé and Laurence Cars, Correspondances Musée d'Orsay Art Contemporain no. 7: Brice Marden/Gustave Courbet, Paris: Musée d'Orsay and Argol Éditions, 2006, p.30. | E. Costello, Brice Marden, London, New York: Phaidon Press, 2013, p. 56. | M. Stone, "Brice Marden The Seventies", Henri, 29 May 2020. | | The present lot is an unequivocally unique work in which the viewer's experience transcends any written articulation of its beauty. Painted by Brice Marden in 1967, Flesh is one of only seven works that make up the rare Back Series completed by the artist in 1967-68 and has an extraordinary history of ownership, including the personal collection of Andy Warhol. The seven works that make up this series are deeply personal and embody Marden's visionary approach to abstract painting. It is no coincidence that each painting in this series is the same height, 69 inches, as the artist's wife and fellow painter, Helen Marden, who remained a steadfast influence on her husband for the entirety of his career. With a gentle, yet assertive hand, Marden rendered surfaces of amazing complexity. Though each brush stroke was deeply considered, Marden's monochrome paintings are vast landscapes of a particular hue that feels spiritual and instinctive. This is abundantly clear in Flesh in which the unique color emanates from the canvas transforming a combination of inanimate materials (Marden's hallmark use of beeswax and oil paint) into a transcendent and intimate portrait. | | Flesh was a foundational work in the seminal exhibition at the Bykert Gallery in 1968, which displayed each piece from the Back Series and whose announcement card detailed a photo of Helen Marden's back. Flesh underscores, in its intangible effect and poignant title, the throughline of this exhibition in which each painting is, either directly or indirectly, an intimate portrayal of an individual such as For Otis (after Otis Redding) and Nico (after the German singer, actress, and Warhol muse). Said to be painted during a period of distance between the artist and Helen Marden, the Back Series is directly connected to the symbol of one's literal back in which "the idea of rejections – expressed at a primitive and direct level by the turning of one person's back on another – is integral to these paintings" (Linda Shearer, Brice Marden, Brice Marden's Paintings, Exh. Cat., The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, 1975, p. 17). | | It is no coincidence that Marden often worked in a life-size, human, scale in which the abstract becomes corporeal to result in a viewing experience that is not about observing from the outside in but rather the inside out. It is this framework that emphasizes Marden as a painter whose process and artistic undertakings speak to the traditions of painting rather than Minimalism or Post-Minimalism (a movement in which his early works are frequently categorized). As Marden once said, upon seeing Edouard Manet's Street Singer, he "saw the warm umber and the color fell into place it became a total color sensation. Each part built towards this total which came slowly, as if being mysteriously revealed. I try for this in my work" (quoted in Brice Marden, Brice Marden's Paintings, Exh. Cat., The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, 1975, p. 12). | | Marden was a serious student of Art History. As a guard at the Jewish Museum in the early sixties, Marden meditated upon Jasper Johns' 1964 survey exhibition in which he drew inspiration not from Johns' use of language and objects, but rather from his astute painterly character. As Roberta Smith writes, Marden "turned to the history of painting for inspiration, opening up new possibilities for abstraction and beyond [...] He talked, like a traditional painter, of the importance of light and nature and reverentially considered the rectangle one of the great human inventions." ('Brice Marden: A Legacy Beyond the Monochromes', New York Times, 14 August 2023) So, it is no surprise that a work like Street Singer would resonate in Marden's practice as a significant influence. Flesh is a resolute and sublime painting that speaks to the fundamental tenets of Marden's practice that endured for the entirety of the artist's career. | | In a 2009 interview, Gordon Locksley said "Brice Marden changed, for the rest of my life, the way I look at paintings" (quoted in With You I Want to Live: The Collection of Gordon Locksley and George T. Shea, exh. cat. Museum of Art Fort Lauderdale, 2009-10, n.p.). Tastemakers Gordon Locksley and George Shea saw the artistic genius of Marden long before the Art World recognized his brilliance. And now, Marden is celebrated as one of the most important groundbreaking artists of his generation who energized the medium of painting for generations to come. | | Marden received his MFA from Yale University's School of Art and Architecture in 1963 and shortly after secured his first solo exhibition at the legendary Bykert Galley in 1966, while working as Robert Rauschenberg's studio assistant. He has been the subject of numerous significant retrospectives at institutions such as the Hamburger Bohnhoff Museum for Contemporary Art, Berlin; the Museum of Modern Art, New York; the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York; and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Marden's work can be found in countless permanent collections such as the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis; the National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C.; the Art Institute of Chicago; and the Centre Pompidou, Paris amongst others.

title: Untitled (Hudson River Series) (SG-2007-AC-877)
description: Untitled (Hudson River Series) (SG-2007-AC-877) signed and dated 'Sonia Gechtoff 2007' (on the reverse) acrylic on canvas 35 7/8 x 35 7/8 in (91.1 x 91.1 cm) Painted in 2007
provenance: The artist's studio. | Estate of the artist. | Private collection, New York. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. |  |  | The abstract expressionist Sonia Gechtoff, born in Philadelphia, grew up surrounded by the arts as the child of a gallerist mother and an artist father, who first taught her how to paint. Shortly after graduating from the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts in 1950, Gechtoff relocated to the Bay Area where she fell in with fellow Bay Area artists Hassel Smith, Elmer Bischoff, Ernest Briggs and Deborah Remington. She was the subject of the first solo exhibition ever organized for a female abstract expressionist, held at the De Young Museum in 1957. That same year her work appeared alongside that of Clyfford Still and Richard Diebenkorn at the inaugural exhibition at Ferus Gallery. Then in 1958 Gechtoff moved to New York, where she found gallery representation. Throughout her long career she held many teaching appointments at various institutions such as New York University, the National Academy, the Art Institute of Chicago, among others.  |  | A tremendous draughtswoman known for incorporating graphite in her acrylic paintings, Gechtoff innovated a technique using the palette knife at a time when many abstract expressionists were seeking new gestural approaches. One key hallmark of her work beginning in the late 1950s was a slashing approach that resembled a vortex. Critic Dore Ashton described her technique as "a surface similar to the overlapping feathers of a wet bird." Two years before her death she was featured in the groundbreaking exhibition Women of Abstract Expressionism at the Denver Art Museum, held in 2016. More recently in 2023 her work appeared in the Whitechapel exhibition Action, Gesture Paint: Women Artists and Global Abstraction 1940-1970. Her paintings can be found in such notable public collections including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and the Baltimore Museum of Art.

title: Pink, Green
description: Pink, Green oil on canvas 69 5/8 x 27 5/8 in (176.7 x 70.4 cm) Painted in 1965
provenance: The Waddington Galleries, London. | Private collection, London. | Thence by descent to the present owner. | | Literature | S. Stanners (ed.), Jack Bush Paintings: A Catalogue Raisonné, Vol. 2, Toronto, 2004, no. 2.40.1965.100, p. 496 (illustrated p. 497). | | | There is a discernible sensitivity inherent to Jack Bush's canvases that sets him apart from the brazen theatricality of those artists associated with the Washington Color School, and perhaps equally as much from the Painters Eleven, a group of Canadian modernists of whom Bush was a founding member. | | If in the Targets of Kenneth Noland or the Romanesque draperies of Sam Gilliam we find a fanatical vision of what pure abstraction can deliver in space, Bush is the realist whose introspective paintings provide an adagio of shapes and color that speak only for themselves. Pink Green, from 1965, offers a kind of natural haven, indulging the eyes with a slender glimpse onto green quadrants that intuit a reading of the piece as relating to landscape. Such is the painting's chromatic array that the central column's colors are heightened to bring their presence right to the fore of the picture plane. | | Bush was a pure colorist; an artist in the vein of Josef Albers who engaged with color and geometric forms as a kind of psychosomatic stimulant. A professional illustrator for much of his early career, his relationship to abstraction was deeply personal. In the mid-1960s, Bush's practice developed a fuller and more refined identity through the Columns. Moving away from the influence of the New York school, 1965 would be the final year Bush would work in oils and forms the core of a highly accomplished period for the painter. | | Writing on the subject of Colour Column on Suede, also from 1965, that resides in the Tate Gallery collection in London, Bush noted: "It is one of a series I painted during 1964-66 [...] All the canvases in this series were stretched on a false wall, with plenty of extra canvas all round, so as to allow the 'column' or central image, to get itself placed and surrounded, with the 'ground' colour; not a background - but an active-neutral two sides that would bring the 'column' to its greatest pitch in colour. The amount of ground needed seemed crucial, so that the cropping was done only after the canvas was completed. Since then, I have been attempting to make that ground much more active, so that I am ending up with an all over image" (the artist quoted in, R. Alley, Ed., Catalogue of the Tate Gallery's Collection, London 1981, p.81). | | This 'all over image' is wonderfully manifested in Pink, Green, the curtains of 'active-neutral' blue and dusty maroon both expanding the image laterally and defining its verticality. A quintessential example of his Columns, Pink, Green is a supreme example by one of Canada's most esteemed and collectible painters. Completely fresh to market from longstanding family ownership, it represents a splendid opportunity to acquire an unmolested painting by Jack Bush from the prime of his career.
